summary: A booklet of step-by-step scenarios for trying out ARPANET host computers. Using annotated scripts from the MIT-DMCG PDP-10 system, it shows logging in, using simple features, getting online help and chatting with other users, to help newcomers and system programmers.

plainLanguage.summary: A how-to with sample sessions for first-time users. It shows what to type and what the computer says back.

questions: how did people log in to arpanet hosts in 1971
what is the arpanet scenario booklet
subtitle: A booklet of annotated sample sessions for logging in to and trying out ARPANET host computers.

tldr.problem: In October 1971 a newcomer on the ARPANET had many different host computers to try, each with its own login routine and commands, and little guidance on how to start.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is a booklet of annotated scripts, one per host. Each shows what the user types, what the host answers, and comments in parentheses explaining each step.
tldr.outcome: It is a practical how-to rather than a protocol. The RFC does not state what became of it, and its status is listed as Unknown.

facts.label: Author
facts.value: A. K. Bhushan, MIT Project MAC

today: The RFC's status is listed as Unknown, and no RFC obsoletes it or updates it according to the metadata. It is a snapshot of how to use specific hosts in 1971, so the commands in it describe those systems as they were then.

sections.title: Purpose of the Booklet
sections.content:
RFC 254 is a scenario booklet by A. K. Bhushan of MIT Project MAC. Its goal is to help a user sample host computers on the ARPANET and so stimulate interest in using the network.

The scenarios cover the login procedure, some simple or interesting facilities, and on-line help such as documentation and interactive dialog with experienced users through "link" or "message" mechanisms. Where appropriate, each also includes an exercise in editing and running a very simple program.
sections.plainLanguage: The booklet is a set of practice runs. You follow along, step by step, to try out different computers on the network without getting lost.

sections.title: How the Scripts Are Written
sections.content:
The scenarios assume the environment of the MIT-DMCG PDP-10 computer system, but are meant to be adaptable to use from other systems. Each script is annotated: comments are enclosed in parentheses and the user's input is underlined.

A carriage return is shown as <CR>, and a space is shown as a blank. The escape to the local user TELNET is a backslash, the default escape character on the MIT-DMCG system. Blank lines were added in many places to make the scripts easier to read.

A table of contents lists each host computer with its network address, for example UCLA SIGMA at address 1 and MIT PDP-10 (DMCG) at address 70.
sections.plainLanguage: The booklet shows what you type underlined and explains each line in brackets, like a recipe with notes beside every step.

sections.title: What a Session Does
sections.content:
A typical script starts with the user TELNET connecting to a host, then logging in. On the UCLA-NMC SIGMA-7 running SEX, the user logs in as ARPA, reads and sends messages with the MSG program, lists current users with .WHO, and can chat with a question-answering program called TIMMY.

On the SRI NIC machine the user logs in, and can link their console to another user so the two can type to each other. On Multics the user reads help files, sends mail, then creates, compiles and runs a tiny PL/1 program that prints hello, before logging out.

The booklet also shows piggy-back login: connecting from one remote host onward to another through TELNET. The author says this is meant to help system programmers debug and test their protocol implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each practice run goes: say hello to a computer, sign in, try a few things like sending a note or asking who else is there, then sign out.
